definition: The written document that transfers ownership of real property from a grantor to a grantee.
The grantor transfers title and signs the deed; the grantee receives title.
The words of conveyance in a deed, like "grant and convey," showing intent to transfer.
The deed with the most protection: the grantor warrants title against defects from any time, not just their ownership.
A deed in which the grantor warrants only against defects arising during their own ownership.
A deed that transfers whatever interest the grantor has, if any, with no warranties. Often used to clear clouds on title.
A deed with limited implied warranties that the grantor hasn't already conveyed the property and that it's free of undisclosed encumbrances the grantor created.
A formal declaration before a notary that the signature is genuine and voluntary. Required to record, not to make the deed valid.
Title passes when the grantor delivers the deed with intent to transfer and the grantee accepts it.
Filing a document in the county's public records, which gives constructive notice to everyone.
Notice the law presumes everyone has from public records or open possession, whether or not they looked.
Knowledge a person actually has, from seeing, reading or being told.
The recorded history of ownership transfers for a property.
A summary of all recorded documents affecting a property's title.
Insurance protecting against losses from covered title defects that existed before the policy date.
A title policy protecting the buyer, usually for as long as they or their heirs own the property.
A title policy protecting the lender up to the loan balance. It doesn't protect the buyer.
Any claim or document that casts doubt on ownership, like an old unreleased lien.
A lawsuit to resolve competing claims and clear a cloud on title.
Title reasonably free of defects, so a prudent buyer would accept it.
An arrangement where a neutral third party holds funds and documents until the contract's conditions are met.
The neutral party who holds funds and documents and carries out the parties' written instructions.
A debit is a charge to a party; a credit is money owed to or received by that party at closing.
Dividing ongoing costs, like taxes or rent, between buyer and seller by the days each owns the property.
A federal law requiring the buyer to withhold part of the price when the seller is a foreign person, unless an exemption applies.
The IRS form reporting the gross proceeds of a real estate sale, usually filed by the closing agent.
Foreclosure through a court lawsuit, typical with mortgages.
Foreclosure without a court case, through a trustee's sale under a power of sale in a deed of trust.
A borrower's right to stop foreclosure by paying what's owed before the sale.
A court judgment for the amount still owed when a foreclosure sale brings less than the debt, where allowed.
A sale for less than the loan balance, with the lender's approval to accept less.
Property a lender owns after a foreclosure sale fails to attract a buyer.
A borrower deeds the property to the lender to avoid foreclosure.
Gaining title by open, notorious, continuous, hostile and exclusive possession for the period state law sets.
The court process that validates a will, pays debts, and distributes a deceased person's property.
Dying without a valid will. State law decides who inherits.
A gift of real property by will. The recipient is the devisee.
A tax-deferred exchange of investment or business real property for like-kind property.
A federal tax rule letting owners exclude up to $250,000 of gain ($500,000 for most married couples) on a main home lived in 2 of the last 5 years.
The contract between an owner and a property manager, creating a general agency and setting duties and pay.
A property manager's projection of income and expenses for the year.
Scheduled upkeep, like HVAC servicing, that prevents bigger problems.
Repairs to something that's broken.
Handling risk by avoiding it, controlling it, transferring it with insurance, or retaining it.
A lease where the tenant pays a fixed rent and the owner pays the property's expenses. Common for apartments.
A lease where the tenant pays rent plus some or all property expenses. In a triple net lease, the tenant pays taxes, insurance and maintenance.
A retail lease with base rent plus a percentage of the tenant's gross sales.
A long-term lease of land only. The tenant often builds and owns the improvements during the lease.
The tenant rents part or all of the space to someone else for part of the term. The original tenant stays liable to the landlord.
The tenant transfers the entire remaining lease to a new tenant, who then deals with the landlord directly.
Money a tenant pays to secure performance of the lease, refundable less lawful deductions.
A landlord's duty to keep residential property fit to live in.
When a landlord's failure makes the property unusable, letting the tenant leave and stop paying rent.
The legal process through which a landlord removes a tenant, through the courts.
Evicting a tenant for complaining about conditions or exercising legal rights. Prohibited.
A tenant's right to use the property without interference from the landlord.
What the seller keeps: sale price minus commission, loan payoff and other costs.
How a commission is divided between brokerages, and between a broker and a salesperson.
A proration method using 30-day months and a 360-day year.
Paid after the period it covers, like property taxes in many areas. The seller credits the buyer for the unpaid days the seller owned it.
Principal, interest, taxes and insurance: the full monthly housing payment.
Paying off a loan with regular payments covering interest and principal. Early payments are mostly interest.
Interest = principal × rate × time.
Profit or income divided by the amount invested, shown as a percentage.
An increase in property value over time.
A foot of property width along the street. Lots priced by front foot use the street-facing side.
A unit of area equal to 9 square feet.
One-tenth of a cent ($0.001). A tax rate of 1 mill is $1 per $1,000 of assessed value.
The value the tax assessor assigns for property tax purposes, often a percentage of market or taxable value.
A tax charged when real property is conveyed, usually based on the price. Rates and who pays vary by state and county.
